title: Facility support, water hygiene and biological task safety
description: Complete original G22 guided knowledge course: six taught lessons, two fully worked cases and 26 individually explained questions. Practical qualification and employer-specific implementation remain separate.
purpose: Address TG31 foundation knowledge by distinguishing actual facility/water/biological duties and preventing contamination through suitable systems, hygiene and handoff decisions.
practicalBoundary: Foundation only: not a licensed water/treatment operator, plumbing/backflow, clinical, laboratory, confined-space or specialist cleanup qualification. Actual exposure confirmation, system/product methods, appropriate practical assessment and jurisdiction-specific requirements remain separate.

lessons.title: Start here — identify the actual water and biological duty
lessons.body:
# G22 — Facility support, water hygiene and biological task safety

A housing provider, a warehouse clerk, a plumber and a wastewater worker can all appear within a broad facility-support service category. They do not automatically share the same exposure or qualification. A lease does not prove the supplier treats drinking water, and a maintenance role does not automatically include contaminated laundry, sewage entry or clinical care. This course begins by identifying the actual duty and the route by which people could be exposed.

G22 addresses the water-hygiene and broader communicable-exposure foundation identified by TG31. It complements food hygiene G05 and bloodborne-pathogen G04; neither course alone covers every water or facility biological hazard. You will study six taught lessons with six checks, two fully worked fictional cases and twenty final questions. Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation. First-answer and remediated scores remain separate.

The course teaches recognition, prevention, safe handoff and escalation. It supplies no drinking-water release certificate, treatment-operator license, plumbing/backflow qualification, laboratory authority, clinical training or medical advice. Employer/system-specific procedures, actual exposure assessment and appropriate practical capability remain separate. Requirements depend on the work and jurisdiction; no universal treatment dose, flushing duration, disinfectant recipe or water-system operating limit is invented here.

All examples are original fiction. They demonstrate decisions without operating a water system or exposing anyone to contaminated material. The employer and responsible water/facility authorities must establish what applies to the actual people, system and task before assigning work.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — recognize sources, routes and distinct responsibilities
lessons.body:
## A biological concern is not a single hazard category

Biological hazards can involve microorganisms in contaminated water, human waste, bodily material or the environment. Exposure can occur by swallowing contamination from hands or food, splashes to eyes or mouth, contact with damaged skin, or inhaling relevant aerosols. Different tasks create different pathways. A person recording a water-delivery invoice does not necessarily have the same contact as the person connecting a hose or cleaning a sewage-contaminated drain.

Distinguish potable-water hygiene, wastewater/sewage work, building-water systems, ordinary housekeeping, contaminated laundry and personal/clinical care. There can be overlap, but one label does not replace another's assessment. A bloodborne-pathogen program addresses specified blood and other potentially infectious material; it does not automatically control every sewage organism or building-water aerosol. Food hygiene likewise does not qualify someone to repair a potable-water connection.

## Trace what the worker actually touches or changes

Identify the material/system, task, people affected and potential route. Ask whether work could contaminate a clean supply, create splashes, disturb soiled items or expose another crew through a shared space. The absence of odor or visible dirt cannot demonstrate microbiological safety. Conversely, every wet surface is not proof of a particular infection. Preserve the distinction between a suspected exposure pathway and a confirmed diagnosis or laboratory finding.

Use the service definition as a starting point, then confirm the person's actual duties. Broad property, accommodation, storage or support contracts need decomposition. Select additional training only where the role and exposure are established; do not assign clinical care or sewage-handling qualification merely because a company rents housing.

## Worked example: the camp office and the drain crew

Talia handles room bookings. A separate contractor clears a backed-up sanitary drain. Talia needs to know the restricted area, reporting and access arrangements, but the booking role does not authorize drain clearing. The drain crew needs an actual contamination and physical-hazard assessment, suitable method and prepared personnel. A supervisor who asks Talia to mop the overflow has changed her duty and must resolve readiness before she handles contaminated material.

A sound record states what is known and what remains uncertain. Do not write a guessed disease name to make the concern seem serious. Describe the overflow, affected surfaces, contact routes and protective restriction so the appropriate facility or health authority can make the next decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — protect drinking-water identity and connections
lessons.body:
## Clear appearance does not establish potability

Drinking water must come through an appropriate approved supply and handling arrangement. Rainwater, process water, fire-system water and wastewater are not automatically suitable for drinking, food work or personal washing. Water can be clear while unsuitable. The responsible authority determines applicable water-quality requirements and restrictions; a worker must not make a release decision from taste, odor or a photograph.

Maintain the identity and separation of potable and nonpotable supplies. Use suitable designated containers, hoses, fittings and connection procedures. A hose previously used in a contaminated service does not become drinking-water equipment just because the outside is washed. Keep outlets and containers protected from contamination, and prevent users confusing nonpotable outlets with the drinking supply. Shared dipping utensils or an open pail can introduce contamination into otherwise suitable water.

## Recognize a cross-connection

A cross-connection is an actual or potential link between a potable system and another source that could contaminate it. Backflow can occur when pressure relationships change. For example, immersing a supply hose in a contaminated tank can create a potential pathway back toward the clean system under adverse conditions. Do not assume current forward flow proves the arrangement remains safe.

The correct protection depends on the actual installation and governing requirements. A competent plumbing/water authority determines suitable separation or backflow protection and any testing needed. This course does not tell an unqualified worker which assembly to install or certify. If the connection cannot be verified, hold the affected use and obtain authorized resolution rather than rely on a convenient adapter.

## Worked example: the borrowed fill hose

A camp needs additional water quickly. Someone proposes filling its drinking-water storage using a hose previously used for drain cleaning and a connection whose protection is unknown. The receiver declines the unsupported arrangement and contacts the responsible supply/facility role. They obtain a suitable approved alternative or keep the affected supply restricted. Buying fresh bottled water for immediate needs can be considered through the approved contingency, but it does not by itself correct the connection hazard.

For a water advisory, follow the actual issuer's instructions and employer response. Boiling is not a universal remedy for every chemical or biological concern, and this course supplies no substitute treatment procedure. Communicate which uses are restricted, what alternative is authorized and who can clear the restriction.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — understand building-water stagnation and aerosol concerns
lessons.body:
## Water quality can change inside a building

An approved incoming supply does not guarantee every downstream outlet remains controlled indefinitely. Storage, low use, building shutdown, equipment changes and poor maintenance can alter the conditions in a water system. A long-closed camp wing, an infrequently used outlet or a cooling-water system may need attention under the applicable management program before normal use resumes.

Legionella is an example of a water-associated hazard requiring a suitable management approach. Building systems can support growth and spread under certain conditions, and exposure can involve inhalation of contaminated water aerosols. This is different from treating every water concern as a bloodborne event or assuming the only route is drinking. The actual system and use determine what needs competent review.

## Follow the water-management program rather than improvise

A suitable program identifies the system, hazards, control measures, monitoring, corrective responses and verification responsibilities. The facility's technical team determines relevant operating conditions and methods. A general cleaner or receptionist should not change hot-water settings, dose chemicals or perform an improvised system flush. Such actions can introduce scalding, chemical, aerosol or other exposures and may not address the underlying system.

Monitoring values must be interpreted within the actual program. A single result at one outlet is not automatically proof that every branch, tank or device is suitable. Distinguish a planned inspection, an actual check and the responsible release decision. If a required condition is unknown or a control fails, restrict the affected use through the appropriate authority and investigate the specific system.

## Worked example: reopening an unused annex

A housing manager reopens an annex after a long closure. The main camp remained occupied, so someone assumes the annex water needs no separate review. The manager checks the actual reopening and water-management arrangements with the responsible facility team before dependent use. The team evaluates the annex's real conditions and required controls instead of borrowing the main building's status.

The completion record should describe what was assessed, corrected and verified and which uses are released. A statement that a tap ran clear does not establish microbiological safety or competent system commissioning. Communicate remaining restrictions to cleaners, maintenance staff and occupants. G22 supports recognizing this readiness gap; it does not qualify Legionella system assessment, water treatment or specialist sampling.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — handle sewage, drains and wastewater without creating exposure
lessons.body:
## Recognize both biological and physical hazards

Human waste and sewage can contain organisms capable of causing illness. Exposure can occur during splashing, handling contaminated tools or touching the face with soiled hands. A worker can transfer material to food, a vehicle or a clean room after leaving the immediate task. Wastewater treatment or dilution does not justify assuming all biological hazards have disappeared.

Sewage-related work can also involve hazardous atmospheres, oxygen deficiency, moving equipment, pressure, electricity, unstable surfaces or concealed sharps. A drain, sump, tank or pit may need confined-space assessment. Do not enter, lean into an unassessed opening or attempt a rescue on the basis of this hygiene course. Odor cannot verify atmospheric safety, and a general face covering cannot supply respiratory or rescue qualification.

## Establish the handling and hygiene arrangement first

Use a task assessment and suitable controlled method. Protect bystanders, arrange appropriate equipment, minimize avoidable splashing and maintain clean/contaminated boundaries. Select protective clothing, gloves, footwear and splash protection from the actual exposure and other hazards. Workers need to know how to use and remove their assigned PPE without transferring contamination.

Provide appropriate handwashing and clean welfare arrangements. Wash hands with soap and safe water after the relevant handling and after PPE removal, and before eating or drinking. Keep soiled equipment and workwear from clean cabins and food areas through the designated handling route. Do not eat, smoke or handle a phone with contaminated hands. PPE is not a reason to reach blindly into waste or compress a bag that could contain a sharp.

## Worked example: a backed-up sump near the break area

An overflow reaches a walkway beside a break cabin. A worker proposes pushing it toward a storm drain with a pressure hose. The supervisor stops the unsupported method, controls access and obtains the appropriate facility/environmental response. The assessment must address source control, contamination, runoff and any aerosol generation; relocating waste into another drainage system is not automatically a safe correction.

The team identifies the prepared personnel and approved disposal/decontamination arrangements. If a sharp or unknown material is found, the task is reassessed rather than handled by guesswork. Clinical advice about immunization or health conditions belongs with appropriate professionals; this course does not prescribe vaccines or decide individual fitness for sewage duties.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — control facility cleaning, laundry and shared-contact pathways
lessons.body:
## Cleaning and disinfecting are different actions

Cleaning removes soil and reduces contamination. Disinfection uses an appropriate product and method against relevant microorganisms on suitable surfaces. A visibly tidy room is not proof that the required infection-control process was completed. Conversely, indiscriminate disinfectant use is not always the appropriate response to every ordinary surface. Follow the facility's actual risk-based procedure and any specific setting requirements.

Read the product instructions, including intended use, material compatibility, protective measures and required application conditions. Do not mix cleaning chemicals or invent a stronger concentration. A product appropriate for one surface or organism may not be appropriate for another. Keep food, clean laundry and personal items protected from cleaning chemicals. Healthcare and specialized care settings can require controls beyond ordinary community-building guidance.

## Prevent transfer across the clean boundary

Plan handling so tools, cloths, carts and PPE do not carry contamination from toilets or affected rooms into clean areas. Gloves can contaminate door handles and radios; they do not make every touched object clean. Use suitable task transitions and hand hygiene. For some communicable illnesses, hand sanitizer alone is not a substitute for soap-and-water washing; norovirus is an important example. The employer's actual procedure must address relevant exposure rather than rely on one universal hygiene product.

Handle soiled laundry under the designated method, avoiding unnecessary disturbance and keeping its identity and containment intact. A routine linen service is different from handling blood-soiled items or material associated with a suspected infectious event. Refer bloodborne exposures to the G04/employer program and food-handling issues to the G05/food program where relevant. Do not treat those overlaps as clinical qualification.

## Worked example: shared cleaning equipment

A cleaner uses a cart and cloths in an area affected by vomiting, then prepares to clean dining-room tables without the required transition. A colleague stops the transfer and the responsible person applies the appropriate cleaning, disinfection, equipment and affected-surface response. Replacing the cloth alone may leave the cart, gloves or touched handles unresolved. The team checks actual pathways rather than simply adding a completed-room tick.

Report relevant symptoms or contamination concerns through the designated route. Management should arrange safe work and suitable coverage without asking staff to hide illness. Only appropriate clinical/public-health roles determine diagnoses and any individual medical decisions; an administrator should not circulate a person's health details as a cleaning instruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — coordinate safe release, exposure response and public-health interfaces
lessons.body:
## Transfer a usable operating status

A facility handoff should identify the affected system or area, known concern, immediate restriction, work performed, pending verification and the responsible release authority. A maintenance invoice, a closed cleaning task or a photograph of clear water is not enough. The receiver needs to know which uses are permitted and which remain restricted, especially across night shifts, contractors and occupant changes.

Separate correction of a physical defect from verification of water or biological control. Repairing a broken pipe may not establish that the affected supply is ready for drinking. Removing visible sewage may leave contaminated surfaces or an unresolved drainage source. Appropriate competent personnel determine what checks and release conditions apply. A worker should not waive a missing condition because occupants are arriving or another crew needs the room.

## Respond promptly without diagnosing

For possible exposure or illness, use the established care/emergency route and appropriate immediate instructions. Give responders factual information: location, task, material or system known/uncertain, contact route and actions taken. Protect other people from the same hazard through safe authorized measures. Do not delay care to identify an organism or complete a routine report, and do not enter an unsafe space to retrieve a sample.

A suspected cluster of illness or water-quality concern may require public-health, water-authority or environmental coordination. The responsible organization determines applicable notifications and manages the response. Workers should report accurate observations without claiming an outbreak is confirmed or attributing disease to a person. Preserve relevant supply, maintenance, room/use and event records through the authorized process. Medical and identifying information needs appropriately restricted handling.

## Worked example: a repair without a release

Maintenance repairs a water-system defect before shift end and sends a message saying fixed. The receiving supervisor still has an active restriction on drinking use and no verification from the designated authority. They maintain the restriction, arrange the approved alternative and obtain the actual status. They do not treat the repair message as a water-quality certificate.

After a supported release, communicate it to affected users and preserve its basis. Later follow-up should examine whether the control works and the handoff remains reliable. Counting maintenance tickets or noting that nobody complained cannot prove the water-management or hygiene program is effective in the relevant conditions.

lessons.title: Two facility-support cases and fully worked solutions
lessons.body:
## Case 1: reopened housing and the borrowed hose

A camp reopens a long-unused housing annex. The main camp's water service has remained in use, and management assumes this covers the annex. Additional water is needed, so a worker proposes a hose previously used for drain work. The hose's connection to the potable system has not been assessed. A tap in the annex runs clear. Occupants are due to arrive that evening, and the property supplier says its rental contract means every water-system duty is already accepted.

### Worked solution: separate the contract from the tasks

A property rental does not establish who operates, maintains or verifies the water system. Identify the actual facility owner/operator and competent water-management roles, plus what the supplier has contracted to provide. The person coordinating rooms should not become a treatment operator or backflow tester by assumption. Keep dependent uses restricted while the specific readiness questions are resolved through those responsible roles.

The main camp's operating history does not by itself verify an annex after extended low use. The facility team applies the actual reopening and water-management arrangements to the annex. Clear appearance is not microbiological release evidence. G22 supplies no flushing duration, disinfectant dose or temperature setting; competent system-specific instruction must determine the actual method and its safety controls.

### Worked solution: protect the supply connection

Do not use the drain-service hose or unverified connection as the drinking-water arrangement. Contamination can enter through equipment condition or a cross-connection/backflow pathway. Obtain suitable designated supply equipment and the appropriate technical review. Current forward flow or a convenient adapter does not prove protection under changed pressure conditions. An unqualified worker does not certify an assembly or improvise its design.

Use the approved contingency for drinking and other affected needs while the system is unready. Communicate the actual restricted uses to occupants and cleaners; do not issue a generic boil instruction for an unknown concern. The eventual release should identify the system/uses, checks and responsible authority. A rental invoice, repair receipt or photograph of a clear tap cannot replace that decision.

### Later follow-up

Review whether annex reopening is recognized in planning, whether clean supply equipment remains segregated and whether responsibility is explicit in the contract and shift handoff. Observe a later representative delivery or reopening check where appropriate. A new hose purchase is useful progress but does not prove the full connection and water-management system works.

## Case 2: sewage overflow and a shared laundry route

A sanitary drain backs up beside a laundry room. A worker tries to move soiled linen across the wet area, while another proposes washing the overflow into a nearby surface-water drain. Cleaning staff have ordinary housekeeping instruction but no established contaminated-cleanup method for this event. A nearby sump cover is open, and a supervisor suggests looking inside to find the blockage. Several occupants report stomach symptoms, but no diagnosis is established.

### Worked solution: stop the exposure pathways

Control access to the affected area, protect the clean laundry route and notify the responsible facility/environmental roles. Do not flush sewage into another drainage system or create uncontrolled splashing. Do not inspect an unassessed sump by entry or unsafe approach; biological hygiene knowledge does not resolve atmosphere, confined-space or physical hazards. Obtain a suitable assessed method and prepared personnel for source control and cleanup.

Separate ordinary laundry from material whose handling conditions have changed. Keep soiled items appropriately contained and use the designated route so carts, gloves and footwear do not spread contamination into clean storage or dining areas. A label saying dirty is not proof that a leaking bag is adequate containment. If blood, sharps or another special hazard is found, reassess and invoke the applicable program rather than assume one general procedure covers everything.

### Worked solution: support care and accurate reporting

Arrange appropriate care/referral for reported symptoms and provide factual information through the authorized route. Do not diagnose norovirus or another illness from the pattern alone, and do not dismiss the reports because workers cannot identify an organism. The responsible health/public-water/environmental roles determine what investigation and notifications apply. Keep personal clinical details restricted while sharing necessary area and task restrictions with operational staff.

### Worked solution: verify release and lasting control

The competent response addresses the drainage source, contaminated area, equipment/linen pathways and any affected water or welfare use. The area is not ready merely because visible water is gone. Obtain the required completion and release evidence and communicate it to the next shift. Record what remains uncertain rather than writing an unsupported all-clear.

Review the failed drainage, access planning and missing event-specific worker preparation. Later follow-up should examine the actual collection/handling route and response arrangement, not simply count cleaning supplies ordered. Preserve the original event and decisions so recurrent problems remain visible. A completed G22 quiz helps knowledge; it does not establish that the facility system has been corrected or that anyone is qualified for entry, treatment or clinical work.

lessons.title: Final assessment — twenty water and biological decisions
lessons.body: Answer all twenty final questions individually using the actual task, exposure route and authority described. First responses remain recorded. For an incorrect answer, read and explicitly acknowledge the specific correction. All six checks and twenty final questions require correct answers or acknowledged remediation; the remediated score does not overwrite the original score.

lessons.title: Finish — retain the employer, operator and clinical boundaries
lessons.body:
## What guided completion shows

Completion requires all 26 answered correctly or acknowledged remediation, with first-answer and remediated scores retained separately. You have studied task recognition and safe judgment for water and facility biological concerns. The fictional cases are not real company implementation evidence or records of a practical observation.

## What the employer must supply

Confirm actual duties and exposure for the particular people rather than assigning every TG31 service the union of water, sewage, laundry and care duties. Establish the applicable system procedures, clean/contaminated boundaries, protective equipment, suitable supplies, emergency arrangements and release roles. Food safety G05 and bloodborne G04 apply to their actual task overlaps; they do not replace water-management or broader biological controls.

Use appropriately qualified personnel for drinking-water treatment, sampling interpretation, plumbing/backflow decisions, confined-space work and specialist cleanup. Legal licensing or credentials depend on the actual duty and jurisdiction, and this course grants none. Clinical assessment, vaccination advice, treatment and public-health conclusions remain with qualified professionals. G22 is not medical advice or a licensed-operator qualification.

## Separate practical preparation

An appropriate assessor should observe relevant safe skills using controlled tasks or suitable simulation: identifying potable/nonpotable equipment, recognizing an uncertain connection, preventing contaminated-to-clean transfer, using assigned PPE and hygiene methods, and communicating a hold and release accurately. Do not intentionally contaminate water, create a sewage exposure or enter an unsafe space to test a learner. Record unassessed capabilities and arrange further instruction before expanding duties.

Technical water limits, flushing/treatment methods, disinfectant conditions and testing/release criteria must come from the actual competent program. Unknown conditions remain unverified until properly resolved. A course pass, a busy camp or a favorable company score cannot authorize an unsupported drinking-water or facility all-clear.

questions.prompt: A company rents housing. Does that alone establish that its staff handle sewage or provide clinical care?

options.label: No; identify the actual contracted duties, people and exposures.
Yes; every facility-support service includes every biological task.
Yes; the category replaces practical qualification.

questions.prompt: A clear-looking water supply has uncertain source and connection protection. What is appropriate?

options.label: Approve it because it looks clear.
Restrict the affected use and obtain competent verification through the water/facility process.
Taste it to establish safety.

questions.prompt: A long-unused annex is reopening. Can the main building's normal operation automatically clear its water use?

options.label: Yes; all connected outlets remain verified forever.
Yes; any clear tap is a certificate.
No; apply the actual reopening and water-management review to the annex.

questions.prompt: Sewage has overflowed near a break area. Is hosing it into a storm drain an automatic safe correction?

options.label: No; control access and obtain the assessed facility/environmental response.
Yes; moving it out of sight completes control.
Yes; pressure washing removes every other hazard.

questions.prompt: A contaminated cleaning cart is about to enter a clean dining area. What is appropriate?

options.label: Change only the room label.
Stop the transfer and apply the required equipment/PPE/hygiene transition.
Assume gloves make all touched objects clean.

questions.prompt: A water repair message says fixed, but a drinking-use restriction has not been cleared. What should the receiver do?

options.label: Treat the repair message as a water-quality certificate.
Let arriving occupants decide.
Maintain the restriction and obtain the actual authorized release status.

questions.prompt: Which is a possible biological exposure route during waste handling?

options.label: Transfer from contaminated hands to the mouth or food.
Only reading a room-booking record.
Only seeing a sealed clean supply.

questions.prompt: Does bloodborne-pathogen awareness control every sewage or building-water hazard?

options.label: Yes; all biological hazards are identical.
No; the actual sources, routes and programs can differ.
Yes; it automatically grants treatment-operator authority.

questions.prompt: A label says nonpotable water. What should a worker avoid?

options.label: Maintaining its identity and separation.
Asking the responsible authority about permitted uses.
Assuming it is suitable for drinking or personal washing because it is clear.

questions.prompt: What is a cross-connection concern?

options.label: A potential path from another source into a potable system under adverse flow/pressure conditions.
Only a visibly dirty faucet handle.
A guarantee that normal forward flow can never change.

questions.prompt: May a drain-cleaning hose automatically be used to fill drinking-water storage after an external rinse?

options.label: Yes; a rinse proves its entire history and condition.
No; use a suitable designated supply and verified connection arrangement.
Yes; matching fittings establish potability.

questions.prompt: Is boiling a universal response to any water advisory?

options.label: Yes; it fixes every chemical and biological problem.
Yes; it replaces competent release of the system.
No; follow the actual issuer's restrictions and approved contingency.

questions.prompt: What can change water conditions inside a facility?

options.label: Storage, low use, shutdown or changes in system operation and maintenance.
Only the supplier's invoice format.
Nothing after an approved source is connected.

questions.prompt: Why can Legionella require a different exposure assessment from a simple drinking-water assumption?

options.label: It is always the same as a bloodborne puncture.
Relevant exposure can involve water aerosols and particular building systems.
It can be diagnosed from water color.

questions.prompt: Who should determine a building-water treatment or flushing method?

options.label: Any receptionist who has read G22.
The person who guesses the strongest chemical dose.
The appropriately competent facility/water-management process.

questions.prompt: Does one favorable check at one outlet automatically verify every tank and branch?

options.label: No; evidence must be interpreted within its actual system and sampling scope.
Yes; any passing value is universal.
Yes; no program review is needed afterward.

questions.prompt: A sump is open beside sewage work. Does hygiene training authorize inspection by entry?

options.label: Yes; a face covering qualifies entry.
No; space, atmosphere and physical hazards need their own assessment and authorization.
Yes; lack of odor proves a safe atmosphere.

questions.prompt: What helps interrupt contamination transfer after sewage handling?

options.label: Eating with the same contaminated gloves.
Using the work cab as a contaminated-clothing store by default.
Appropriate PPE removal, handwashing and separation from clean welfare areas.

questions.prompt: Is a glove permission to reach blindly into a waste bag?

options.label: No; a concealed sharp or other hazard remains possible.
Yes; every glove is puncture-proof.
Yes; the bag's contents no longer matter.

questions.prompt: How do cleaning and disinfection differ?

options.label: A tidy appearance proves both are complete.
Cleaning removes soil; appropriate disinfection addresses relevant remaining microorganisms under product conditions.
Using the strongest-smelling chemical replaces both.

questions.prompt: What should a worker do about disinfectant mixing and concentration?

options.label: Combine cleaners to make them stronger.
Borrow a recipe from an unrelated surface or organism.
Follow the actual suitable product instructions and facility procedure; do not improvise mixtures.

questions.prompt: For norovirus prevention, is hand sanitizer alone a substitute for soap-and-water handwashing?

options.label: No; follow the appropriate handwashing and task hygiene arrangements.
Yes; one sanitizer controls every organism in every setting.
Yes; gloves also remove all need for handwashing.

questions.prompt: A routine linen contract receives newly contaminated material. What is appropriate?

options.label: Assume every linen task is unchanged.
Review the changed exposure, containment and handling method before unsupported duties.
Send it home with a worker to avoid a delay.

questions.prompt: Several occupants report stomach symptoms. What should operational staff do?

options.label: Declare a specific outbreak from the reports alone.
Dismiss the concern until workers identify an organism.
Arrange appropriate care/reporting and provide facts without diagnosing or disclosing unnecessary clinical details.

questions.prompt: In Case 1, which fact independently clears drinking use of the annex?

options.label: None of the rental invoice, main-camp history or clear tap substitutes for the actual authorized release.
The rental invoice alone.
A photograph of clear water alone.

questions.prompt: In Case 2, what best tests lasting correction?

options.label: Only the number of cleaning supplies ordered.
Later real handling/access arrangements prevent spread and communicate actual restrictions and release.
Only whether a worker passed the quiz.

explanations.G22_check1: Broad service categories do not establish actual exposure or authority. Decompose the work and assign preparation to the real task and role.
explanations.G22_check2: Appearance and taste cannot establish microbiological safety or connection suitability. Use the actual approved supply and release process.
explanations.G22_check3: Low use and system conditions can differ. The actual facility team must evaluate and release the affected system under its program.
explanations.G22_check4: The proposed method can create spread, runoff or aerosol exposure. Resolve source control, handling and disposal through suitable competent arrangements.
explanations.G22_check5: Carts, tools and gloves can transfer contamination. Address the actual pathways, not only visible room cleanliness.
explanations.G22_check6: A physical repair and supported water-use release are different decisions. Preserve the restriction until its actual prerequisites and authority are established.
explanations.G22_final1: Contact pathways depend on actual handling. Contaminated hands can transfer material to ingestion routes; administrative association alone does not establish that exposure.
explanations.G22_final2: Bloodborne, sewage, food and building-water hazards have distinct scope and controls. Overlap does not make one foundation a universal qualification.
explanations.G22_final3: Nonpotable identity must be respected. Appearance cannot turn it into an approved supply for drinking or other protected uses.
explanations.G22_final4: A connection can permit backflow under changed conditions. Competent assessment determines suitable protection; present flow does not prove permanent safety.
explanations.G22_final5: External cleanliness and matching fittings do not establish hygienic suitability or backflow protection. Obtain the actual approved arrangement.
explanations.G22_final6: Different advisories and contaminants require different responses. This course does not supply a universal treatment remedy.
explanations.G22_final7: Downstream systems can change conditions after supply entry. The relevant management program must consider the actual installation and use.
explanations.G22_final8: The actual system and aerosol route matter. Do not reduce every water-associated hazard to ingestion or infer a diagnosis from appearance.
explanations.G22_final9: System methods can create scalding, chemical and aerosol risks. They need actual technical instructions and suitable capability; the foundation supplies no operating recipe.
explanations.G22_final10: A result supports the scope actually checked. Competent interpretation and the relevant release criteria remain necessary for the affected system.
explanations.G22_final11: Biological hygiene does not resolve confined-space, atmosphere or energy hazards. Keep clear and obtain the proper competent arrangement.
explanations.G22_final12: Control continues when leaving the task. Soiled hands, clothing and equipment can spread material to food, vehicles and other people.
explanations.G22_final13: PPE has limits. Use the actual handling method and do not assume a glove eliminates hidden sharp or contact hazards.
explanations.G22_final14: The actions and required conditions differ. Apply the actual facility/product procedure instead of equating visual cleanliness or odor with a completed control.
explanations.G22_final15: Product suitability and conditions matter. Improvised mixing can create chemical hazards and may not control the intended organism.
explanations.G22_final16: CDC distinguishes norovirus control from relying on sanitizer alone. Use suitable handwashing and the actual program rather than a universal product assumption.
explanations.G22_final17: Material and handling changes can introduce different exposure. Establish a suitable prepared arrangement and keep contamination out of clean/home spaces.
explanations.G22_final18: Prompt factual escalation supports professional assessment. Workers should neither make unsupported diagnoses nor delay response because the cause is uncertain.
explanations.G22_final19: Commercial and visual facts do not establish the annex's water-management or connection prerequisites. Obtain the relevant competent evidence and release.
explanations.G22_final20: Effectiveness concerns the operational pathways and handoff. Purchasing or knowledge completion alone does not prove the facility response and hygiene controls work.
